## Phase 5.J236 — Queue/grab POST endpoints (audit row C.1.i-follow-5c closed) — 2026-05-26

Second of the 3 real-work follow-up rows from J234. Ports POST /api/v3/queue/grab/{id} + POST /api/v3/queue/grab/bulk — the user-driven pending-release grab action surfaced by the queue UI when a release is held pending (download client busy, delay profile gating, etc.).

C# reference: src/Sonarr.Api.V3/Queue/QueueActionController.cs:24-55. Single + bulk variants. The C# version awaits _downloadService.DownloadReport(remoteEpisode, null) per id; on first NotFoundException the bulk short-circuits.

Go-port pipeline per id:

  1. Lookup the pending release row via PendingReleaseLookup (narrow interface; *pendingreleases.Repo satisfies via embedded *repo.Repository[Release].Get).
  2. Deserialise the persisted ReleaseInfo column (JSON-marshaled parser.ReleaseInfo from when the row was added).
  3. Deserialise ParsedEpisodeInfo column (JSON parser.ParsedEpisodeInfo; empty/malformed = zero value, non-fatal — dispatch path only reads Release for protocol+URL).
  4. Resolve Series row via QueueGrabSeriesLookup (narrow; *series.Service.GetSeries satisfies). SeriesID=0 or nil-lookup tolerated; dispatcher works without it for non-qBittorrent clients.
  5. Build minimal *decisionengine.Subject: Release + ParsedEpisodeInfo + Series + DownloadAllowed=true (the True flag is required to clear ProcessDecisions isQualified gate; pending releases come from approved-but-deferred decisions so re-approval here is structurally correct).
  6. Wrap in decisionengine.NewDecision (no Rejections — approved by virtue of being on the pending queue).
  7. Dispatch via QueueGrabDispatcher.ProcessDecisions (narrow; *download.ProcessDownloadDecisions satisfies). Returns *ProcessedDecisions which classifies the outcome (Grabbed/Pending/Rejected); not surfaced to the caller — matches C# which returns new { } regardless of dispatch outcome (per-outcome feedback flows via SignalR broadcasts and history events, not the HTTP response).
  8. Respond 200 + {} matching C# return shape.

Episodes deferred: the dispatcher reads only Subject.Release for the actual grab request (URL+protocol). Post-grab history stamping reads ParsedEpisodeInfo + Series at history-write time via the existing trackeddownloads/history seam, so re-resolving Episode rows from ParsedEpisodeInfo at grab time is unnecessary. Documented in handler doc-comment.

Bulk semantics: iterates ids; first ErrNotFound short-circuits to 404 matching C# first-throw-wins. Mid-batch grab failures dont rollback earlier dispatches — same as C# (sequential await, no transactional bracket).

Wiring: added one new parameter to buildHostServer + v3Routes signatures: processDownloadDecisions *download.ProcessDownloadDecisions. main.go call site updated to pass the existing processDownloadDecisions instance constructed at line 2714. Two route bindings added in v3Routes between DELETE /queue/{id} and the existing /queue/bulk DELETE.

Test coverage (queue_grab_test.go, 9 tests):
  - HappyPath: full pipeline + verifies dispatched Subject shape (Release.Title, Release.DownloadURL, Series.Title, DownloadAllowed=true).
  - NotFound404: empty pending repo → 404.
  - InvalidID400: alpha id → 400.
  - PendingGetErr500: db-down → 500.
  - NilSeriesLookupTolerated: SeriesID=0 row → 200 + dispatch (Subject.Series=nil).
  - Bulk HappyPath: two ids → 2 dispatcher calls + 200 + {}.
  - Bulk FirstMissing404ShortCircuits: [99, 2] → 404 + 0 dispatcher calls (first-miss short-circuit).
  - Bulk MalformedBody400: non-JSON body → 400.
  - Bulk EmptyIds200NoDispatch: empty ids array → 200 + 0 dispatches (matches C# zero-iteration).

Hard gates clean: go build ./... no errors, go test ./... 0 FAIL, golangci-lint run ./internal/api/v3/... ./cmd/sonarr/... 0 issues (gofmt auto-fix applied once to align a struct-field comment).

Net diff: ~200 internal/api/v3/queue_grab.go (new file) + ~250 internal/api/v3/queue_grab_test.go (new file with fakes + 9 tests) + ~4 cmd/sonarr/host_wiring.go (1 new import + 1 new param + 1 call-site update + 2 new route lines) + ~3 cmd/sonarr/main.go (1 call-site update) + ~3 PROGRESS.md + ~30 STATUS.md slice note + ~2 AUDIT_FIX_BACKLOG.md (row strikethrough + CLOSED summary).

Read/write balance: this is WRITE side — DELETE is state-changing, dispatching a download is even more so. The matching pending-release read path was already in place (queue_status.go via pendingCountLister). The dispatch itself fires SignalR events (via the existing ProcessDecisions bus integration) so the React UI receives the update without re-polling.

Second of the 3 real-work follow-up rows from J234. Ports POST /api/v3/release + POST /api/v3/release/push, the two write-side endpoints in the indexer-release surface. C# references: src/Sonarr.Api.V3/Indexers/ReleaseController.cs (manual download) + ReleasePushController.cs (Newznab/Torznab push).

New package — internal/releasecache/:

  TTL-keyed in-memory cache mirroring C# ICached<RemoteEpisode>. The 30-minute default TTL pins against C# ReleaseController.cs:240. Goroutine-safe via sync.RWMutex; lazy eviction on Get (no background sweeper since cache size is bounded by search-fanout cadence × TTL). Key format <indexerID>_<guid> matches C# GetCacheKey. Injectable clock for deterministic tests. ~165 LOC + ~150 LOC tests including a -race sweep with 50 concurrent writers and 50 concurrent readers.

POST /api/v3/release (ReleaseDownloadHandler):

  Cache-lookup path. Body: {indexerId, guid, downloadClient, downloadClientId, shouldOverride, seriesId, episodeId, episodeIds, quality, languages}. PostValidator: IndexerId > 0 + Guid non-empty. Cache miss → 404 with the canonical message Couldnt find requested release in cache, try searching again (matches C# wire). Cache hit → ProcessDecisions dispatch + 200 + echo of the request body (matches C# return release). ShouldOverride branch DEFERRED — the C# arm clones the cached RemoteEpisode and mutates Series/Episodes/Quality/Languages from body fields; the Go-port port requires episodes.Service.Get + JSON-deserialise Quality/Languages which the cache itself doesn't carry, and the common UI flow (user clicks Download without override) works without this branch.

POST /api/v3/release/push (ReleasePushHandler):

  Newznab/Torznab push notification entry — 3rd-party indexers drop a release without Sonarr RSS-polling. Body: {title, downloadUrl, magnetUrl, protocol, publishDate, indexer, indexerId, size, infoUrl, commentUrl, downloadClient, downloadClientId}. PostValidator (matches C# ReleasePushController.cs:42-47): Title non-empty + (DownloadUrl OR MagnetUrl non-empty) + Protocol != Unknown + PublishDate != IsZero. Pipeline:

    1. Build synthetic parser.ReleaseInfo (TorrentInfo variant when Protocol=2) with Guid = PUSH-<DownloadUrl> matching C# :59 verbatim.
    2. Run GetRssDecision(ctx, []any{info}, pushedRelease=true) — same path RssSync uses but pushedRelease flag signals to specs that this came from a 3rd-party push (some skip stricter checks).
    3. Empty decision list or nil ParsedEpisodeInfo → 400 with Title: Unable to parse validation failure (matches C# :76-79 guard).
    4. Seed the cache under <IndexerID>_PUSH-<DownloadUrl> so a subsequent POST /release click-to-download finds it.
    5. ProcessDecisions dispatch.
    6. 200 response carrying single-entry list with body fields + Approved/Rejected/Rejections.

  Deferred sub-arcs documented in handler doc-comments:
    (a) Indexer name→id resolve at C# :84-99 (ResolveIndexer). Dispatch works fine with body IndexerID; resolution is for logging consistency.
    (b) DownloadClient name→id resolve at C# :101-115 (ResolveDownloadClientId).

## Phase 5.J238 — POST /api/v3/manualimport reprocess endpoint (audit row C.1.i-follow-5b closed) — 2026-05-26

Third of the 3 real-work follow-up rows from J234, and the final J234-surfaced row. With this closure all 5 originally-numbered C.1.i-follow rows AND all 5 J234-surfaced sub-rows are CLOSED — Phase 5 audit_fix_backlog is fully drained.

Ports the C# `ManualImportController.ReprocessItems` action body of work (the POST verb on /api/v3/manualimport). The C# controller's source: `src/Sonarr.Api.V3/ManualImport/ManualImportController.cs:43`. The endpoint accepts an array of items the UI has already collected (typically from a "Wanted → Cutoff Unmet" or "Activity → Queue" manual-import drawer) and re-derives the per-item Series + Episodes + ReleaseType + (eventually) CustomFormats projection. The UI calls this after the user changes the Series binding or edits the explicit episode list — the server re-walks the precedence rules so the response shows the user what would actually happen on a subsequent /api/v3/manualimport/save POST.

Handler at `internal/api/v3/manual_import.go`:

  The existing v3 file (which previously held only the GET list handler) was extended with: (1) `ManualImportReprocessItem` struct mirroring the C# wire shape (Path, Name, FolderName, IndexerFlags, RelativePath, ReleaseGroup, Quality, Languages, ReleaseType, SeriesId, Series, EpisodeIds, Episodes, CustomFormats, Rejections, DownloadId, AdditionalFile, ReplaceExistingFiles, DisableReleaseSwitching, TitleParse, ParsedEpisodeInfo); (2) two narrow lookup interfaces — `ManualImportSeriesLookup` (Get by ID + GetSeriesByPath) and `ManualImportEpisodeLookup` (Get by ID, used for the explicit-EpisodeIDs resolution arm); (3) the POST `ReprocessItems(ctx, items)` handler; (4) the per-item `reprocessOne` orchestrator; (5) `resolveManualImportSeries` + `resolveManualImportEpisodes` helpers; (6) the `manualImportReleaseTypeFor` helper that derives the wire-format ReleaseType string from `*parser.ParsedEpisodeInfo` shape.

  Per-item precedence rules (line-aligned with C# `:46-90`):

    - Series resolution (C# `:113`): if SeriesId <= 0 AND Path != "" AND series lookup is wired, resolve via GetSeriesByPath (folder-based — the UI hands us the folder, server walks series.Path == folder). Otherwise fall back to ID-based Get if SeriesId > 0. nil-tolerant: missing series + nil-lookup combinations preserve the body-supplied series field.
    - Episode resolution (C# `:51`): explicit EpisodeIDs from the request body take precedence — for each ID, episodeLookup.Get fetches the typed Episode. If EpisodeIDs is empty AND ParsedEpisodeInfo is set AND series resolved, the parsed-info-derived episode stub list is built from the (Season, EpisodeNumber) tuples. The C# tree uses `parsedEpisodeInfo != null ? ... : new List<Episode>()` — the Go-port mirrors this with the empty-EpisodeIDs fallback.
    - ReleaseType derivation (C# `:51` `processedItem.ReleaseType`): new `manualImportReleaseTypeFor(*parser.ParsedEpisodeInfo)` helper applies the upstream `ParsedEpisodeInfo.ReleaseType` getter (C# `Parser/Model/ParsedEpisodeInfo.cs:90-115`): nil parsed-info → `unknown`; `FullSeason → seasonPack`; `len(EpisodeNumbers) >= 2 → multiEpisode`; `== 1 → singleEpisode`; else `unknown`.

  Wire format — camelCase via `CamelCaseEnumName`:

    The Go-port `parser.ReleaseType.String()` emits PascalCase (matches C#'s `Enum.ToString()` raw form). But the v3 API contract emits camelCase enum values — verified against `src/Sonarr.Api.V5/openapi.json` `ReleaseType` schema: `enum: [unknown, singleEpisode, multiEpisode, seasonPack]`. C# achieves camelCase via `[JsonConverter(typeof(StringEnumConverter))]` + the `CamelCaseNamingStrategy` configured in `Sonarr.Http`. The Go-port uses the existing `CamelCaseEnumName` helper (lowercases the first character of the PascalCase name) — same pattern already used in command.go, config_importlist.go, config_host.go for other enum fields. Initial implementation returned `parser.ReleaseType{...}.String()` directly (PascalCase) and 2 tests caught this — fixed by wrapping each return in `CamelCaseEnumName(...)`.

  CustomFormats normalisation (C# null-as-empty JSON projection):

    C# Newtonsoft.Json with the default Sonarr config serialises `null List<CustomFormatResource>` as `[]` (the `Sonarr.Http` JSON contract resolver). Go-port `[]any{}` initialisation when `item.CustomFormats == nil` after the precedence walk matches the wire byte-for-byte. (When the body supplies a non-nil non-empty CustomFormats list, it round-trips verbatim — re-deriving custom-format scores is a separate slice that requires the CustomFormat service to be threaded in.)

Test coverage (`internal/api/v3/manual_import_test.go`, 11 new tests):

  - Empty body → 200 + `[]` (no items, no resolution work, no error).
  - Nil ParsedEpisodeInfo → ReleaseType = `unknown`.
  - FullSeason=true → ReleaseType = `seasonPack`.
  - Single-episode (one EpisodeNumber) → ReleaseType = `singleEpisode`.
  - Multi-episode (E01-E03 spans two episodes per the C# `:51` `len >= 2` rule) → ReleaseType = `multiEpisode`.
  - Explicit EpisodeIDs in body → resolved via episodeLookup.Get for each ID, parsed-info-derived stubs ignored.
  - Empty EpisodeIDs + ParsedEpisodeInfo set + series resolved → parsed-info-derived episode stub list returned.
  - Path-based series lookup (SeriesId <= 0, Path != "", series lookup wired) → GetSeriesByPath invoked.
  - ID-based series lookup (SeriesId > 0, Path empty) → Get(seriesID) invoked.
  - CustomFormats nil → empty-slice normalisation in response.
  - Plus a smoke / route-wiring guard.

Wiring (`cmd/sonarr/host_wiring.go`):

  POST `/api/v3/manualimport` route added next to the existing GET handler. The two narrow interfaces (`ManualImportSeriesLookup`, `ManualImportEpisodeLookup`) are satisfied by `*series.Service` + `*episodes.Service` respectively via Go structural typing — no new wiring params on `buildHostServer` / `v3Routes`. The two services were already threaded into the v3 routes block from earlier slices.

## Phase 5.J239 — Phase 6.1 shadow-traffic harness skeleton — 2026-05-26

First Phase 6 prep slice. The Phase 6 scope doc (PHASE_6_SCOPE.md § 6.1) calls for a reverse-proxy binary that dual-dispatches every API request to both the canonical C# Sonarr backend and the Go-port binary, returns the primary's response to the caller, diffs the secondary's body against the primary post-redaction, and writes daily diff reports grouped by severity. J239 ships that binary at `go/cmd/shadow-traffic-diff/`.

Architecture:

  - `main.go` (~150 LOC) — flag parsing, signal-handling, periodic-flush goroutine, graceful shutdown.
  - `proxy.go` (~250 LOC) — DualProxy http.Handler. Buffers inbound request body once, replays to both backends via goroutines with shared deadline, streams primary's response to caller, kicks off a background diff goroutine after the client stream completes (never blocks the caller's latency).
  - `differ.go` (~120 LOC) — RedactConfig + Differ wrapping the existing normalize package. Severity classification: any KindMissingInA/KindMissingInB/KindTypeMismatch present → HIGH (structural divergence — a real port gap); only KindValueMismatch entries → LOW (likely environmental noise); both bodies byte-equal post-redact → OK.
  - `report.go` (~180 LOC) — in-memory DiffRow + OKBucket buffer + periodic flush to date-stamped JSONL (diffs) + JSON (OK summary) files. Append-mode so service restart doesn't truncate the day's report. RecordOK aggregates byte-equal events into per-(method,path,status) counters.

Refactor — `test/contract/internal/normalize/` → `internal/normalize/`:

  The normalize package was internal to `test/contract/`, blocking import from `cmd/`. Moved to project-level `internal/normalize/` (still internal to the module, but importable from cmd/ and internal/). 4 prior call sites updated: `cmd/shadow-traffic-diff/differ.go` (new), `internal/normalize/diff_test.go`, `test/contract/diff/main.go`, `test/contract/replayer/replayer.go`, `test/contract/internal/runner/runner.go`. Existing contract test suite still passes at the new import path.

Failure-mode handling (per PHASE_6_SCOPE.md operational expectations):

  - Primary unreachable / connection error → return 502 to caller, record HIGH-sev diff with the failure reason. Primary down is the most important shadow-period signal because it breaks the canonical reference.
  - Secondary unreachable / timeout → return primary's response verbatim (caller unaffected), record HIGH-sev diff. The Go port being down doesn't break the canonical surface but does block diff coverage for that request.
  - 200 vs 4xx / 4xx vs 5xx → HIGH-sev (status mismatch always indicates a real port gap).
  - 200 vs 200 byte-equal post-redact → OK aggregate bucket, no per-event row.
  - 200 vs 200 with body diff post-redact:
    - Only KindValueMismatch (e.g. an unredacted timestamp) → LOW.
    - Any KindMissingInA/B or KindTypeMismatch (e.g. Go-port omits a field) → HIGH.

Default RedactConfig (operator override via `-redact-config <file>.json`):

  Conservative baseline covering the dynamic fields already surfaced by the J231/J234 audit slices: system/task `lastDuration` / `nextExecution` / `lastExecution` / `lastStartTime`; command `queued` / `started` / `ended` / `duration` / `stateChangeTime` / `lastExecutionTime`; health `source`; log `records[*].time` / `exception` / `id`; system/status `startTime` / `buildTime` / `runtimeVersion` / `version` / `osVersion` / `osName` / `architecture`; diskspace `freeSpace` / `totalSpace`. New noise discovered during the shadow period gets appended to a deployed `-redact-config` file rather than recompiling the binary.

Test coverage (`proxy_test.go`, 14 tests):

  - End-to-end through the front proxy: byte-equal-no-diff (OK aggregate increments, no diff row); status mismatch HIGH-sev; pure body value diff LOW-sev; missing-field HIGH-sev; secondary-down HIGH-sev; primary-down → 502 to client + HIGH-sev recorded; POST body replayed verbatim to both backends (atomic.Value assertion on each backend's received body); redacted-field difference suppressed (lastDuration values differ but no diff row recorded).
  - Report unit: Flush writes both files; second flush appends to existing files (3 OK bumps → counter=3, 2 DiffRows → 2 JSONL lines).
  - Differ unit: non-JSON body always HIGH-sev (HTML stack trace from a C# 500 catches via this path).
  - Helpers: singleJoin, RedactConfig.RedactPathsFor (empty PathPrefix matches all, prefix-match works, nil-receiver returns nil), LoadRedactConfig (happy + missing-file + malformed-JSON), Severity.String roundtrip.

Hard gates clean: `go build ./...` no errors; `go test ./cmd/shadow-traffic-diff/` 14/14 PASS; `go test -race ./cmd/shadow-traffic-diff/` race-clean; `go test ./internal/normalize/ ./test/contract/...` all green at the new import path.

Net diff: ~150 lines cmd/shadow-traffic-diff/main.go + ~250 cmd/shadow-traffic-diff/proxy.go + ~120 cmd/shadow-traffic-diff/differ.go + ~180 cmd/shadow-traffic-diff/report.go + ~370 cmd/shadow-traffic-diff/proxy_test.go + 4 import path edits + git mv test/contract/internal/normalize → internal/normalize + PROGRESS.md update + STATUS.md slice note.

  - 6.2 smoke runbook — NOT STARTED (operator-driven, not autonomous-loop work).

## Phase 5.J240 — Phase 6.1 production-log replay helper — 2026-05-26

Second Phase 6 prep slice. J239 landed the shadow-traffic-diff binary (the diff side of the harness); J240 lands its replay companion. Together the two binaries form a complete Phase 6.1 toolkit:

  1. Capture a request log somewhere (real Sonarr install via tee tool, manual scripting, or curl-the-corpus).
  2. `shadow-traffic-replay -log capture.jsonl -target http://localhost:9000` feeds the requests into J239's listen addr.
  3. shadow-traffic-diff dispatches each request to both backends in parallel.
  4. Daily diff reports under shadow-reports/.
  5. Operator triages diffs.

Architecture (`go/cmd/shadow-traffic-replay/`):

  - `main.go` (~140 LOC) — flag parsing, signal-handling, periodic stats reporter goroutine, final summary on exit.
  - `log.go` (~180 LOC) — JSONL log format definition (LogEntry struct), streaming LogReader (4 MiB max line for big POST bodies — manualimport / customformat-bulk wouldn't fit the default 64 KiB), Filter struct with method/path-prefix/status matching, ParseStatusFilter helper for the mixed-code-and-class CSV form ("200,4xx,503,5xx").
  - `replay.go` (~250 LOC) — Replayer struct, Stats counter (atomic ints), pacing logic, worker pool, per-request dispatch with header sanitisation (drop hop-by-hop, drop Host, inject Content-Type if Body present and not set, inject User-Agent if missing).

JSONL log format (one object per line):

  Required: method, path. Optional: ts (RFC3339 — used for pacing), headers (map), body (raw string), status (used for filtering).

  Comments (`#` lines) and blank lines are skipped — supports hand-edited test logs without needing a separate tool to strip them.

Pacing model:

  - `-speed 0` → no throttle, fire as fast as the network can carry.
  - `-speed 1.0` (default) → preserve original cadence between entries. Sleep duration = (entry.Timestamp - prev.Timestamp) scaled by 1/Speed.
  - `-speed 10.0` → 10x faster than recorded.
  - `-concurrency N` (N>1) → fan out via worker pool, disables timestamp pacing (parallel workers destroy serial ordering — Speed=0 is the only sensible setting).
  - Entry with zero timestamp → no pacing applied, fires immediately after previous.

Filtering (combined with AND):

  - `-method GET,POST` → method allowlist, case-insensitive exact match.
  - `-path /api/v3/series,/api/v3/episode` → path-prefix allowlist (CSV).
  - `-status 200,4xx,503,5xx` → mixed exact codes + classes. Classes match the N00-N99 range.

Stats (atomic counters):

  - Sent / Filtered / Errors / Status2xx / Status4xx / Status5xx / StatusOther
  - TotalLatency (sum of per-request durations, microseconds) → AvgLatency in snapshot

  Single-line format: `sent=10 filtered=2 errors=0 2xx=8 4xx=1 5xx=1 other=0 avg=1.5ms`. Emitted every -stats-interval (default 5s) + final summary on exit with elapsed + computed rps.

Test coverage (`replay_test.go`, 18 tests):

  - Log parse: happy (3 entries including comment skip), malformed line (error mentions line number), missing required fields.
  - Filter: method allowlist (case-insensitive), path-prefix, status (mixed codes + classes), empty-Filter passes all.
  - ParseStatusFilter: mixed codes + classes round-trip, empty no-error, sub-100 reject ("99" errors), malformed token ("xx2" errors).
  - statusClassMatch boundary tests (199/200/299/300/600 cases).
  - Replayer end-to-end: dispatches each entry to a real httptest server (assertion on count + POST body via sync.Map), preserves query string from path (e.g. `/api/v3/episode?seriesId=1&seasonNumber=2`), respects compound filter (only entries matching BOTH method AND path-prefix pass), paces by timestamp at Speed=2.0 within ±50ms tolerance (skipped on -short), Speed=0 fires 3 entries with 2-second recorded gaps in <500ms wall time, Concurrency=5 max-in-flight assertion (≥2 means parallel actually worked), ctx cancel breaks a long pacing wait within 5s, dispatch error counter on dead-target (127.0.0.1:1), status bucket classification across 200/201/404/500/503/301.
  - Helpers: OpenLogFile happy + missing-file, splitCSV (empty → nil, single, "a, b ,, c" → [a b c]), StatsSnapshot.String formatting.

Hard gates clean: `go build ./...` no errors; `go test ./cmd/shadow-traffic-replay/` 18/18 PASS; `go test -race` race-clean; `go vet` clean.

Net diff: ~140 main.go + ~180 log.go + ~250 replay.go + ~440 replay_test.go + PROGRESS.md update + STATUS.md slice note.

  - 6.1 shadow-traffic harness — toolkit COMPLETE (diff side J239 + replay side J240). Ready to point at staging-host backends with captured traffic.
  - 6.2 smoke runbook — NOT STARTED (operator-driven, not autonomous-loop work).
  - 6.3 nightly contract-suite CI — NOT STARTED (workflow file change only).
  - 6.4 cutover commit — gated on 14+ days of zero unexplained diff in 6.1's daily reports.

## Phase 5.J241 — Phase 6.1 tee/recorder tool — 2026-05-26

Third Phase 6 prep slice. J239 + J240 + J241 form the complete Phase 6.1 toolkit triad:

  1. **shadow-traffic-record (J241)** — captures inbound traffic from a real install into a JSONL log.
  2. **shadow-traffic-replay (J240)** — replays a captured log against any target URL.
  3. **shadow-traffic-diff (J239)** — dual-dispatches inbound traffic to two backends + diffs responses.

Typical Phase 6.1 deployment flow:

  - Day 0: point operator clients at `shadow-traffic-record :9001` fronting C# Sonarr `:8989`. Run normal workflow (add series, search, grab, import). Get `capture.jsonl`.
  - Day 1+: replay capture.jsonl into `shadow-traffic-diff :9000` (which dual-dispatches to C# `:8989` + Go `:8990`). Daily diff reports under `shadow-reports/`.
  - 14+ consecutive days of zero unexplained diff → cutover commit (Phase 6.4).

Architecture (`go/cmd/shadow-traffic-record/`):

  - `main.go` (~120 LOC) — flag parsing, signal-handling, periodic stats reporter, graceful shutdown with writer.Close() drain.
  - `proxy.go` (~130 LOC) — RecordingProxy http.Handler. Single-upstream reverse-proxy that buffers inbound body once, dispatches to upstream, streams response to client via io.Copy (large bodies — full library refresh, log download — not buffered), records the entry AFTER the client stream completes (so the upstream status is known).
  - `writer.go` (~190 LOC) — LogWriter with bounded channel between request hot path and disk drain goroutine. Non-blocking Enqueue (default queue 1024; full → drop + counter bump). Periodic buffered-writer flush (default 2s). Body-length cap with `...<truncated>` marker. Close drains queue + optional fsync. Atomic counters race-clean.

Best-effort capture rationale:

  Under burst load (e.g. UI's initial page load fans out ~20 requests in <100ms) the writer's queue can fill faster than the disk drain goroutine processes it. Two options: (a) block the request hot path waiting for queue space, adding tail latency to inbound traffic; (b) drop the new entry + bump a counter, leaving the request path untouched. Chose (b) — recording proxies that slow down production traffic make operators turn them off. Drop count surfaces in periodic stats so the operator can tell when capture is lossy and either raise -queue-size or accept the loss.

Security: -drop-api-keys default ON:

  Captured logs routinely get emailed, Slacked, checked into PR drafts, etc. Default-deny on X-Api-Key + Authorization headers in the LOG (still preserved upstream-bound so the proxied request authenticates correctly). Test asserts upstream sees the keys + log doesn't. Operators with tightly-controlled replay environments can `-drop-api-keys=false` for fidelity (no current consumer needs this but the flag is there).

Test coverage (`proxy_test.go`, 14 tests):

  - GET happy path: client gets upstream's body verbatim; log captures method+path+query+timestamp+status.
  - POST body verbatim: upstream echoes body back to client (proves proxy forwards it); log captures body byte-for-byte.
  - API key + Authorization stripped from log records, PRESERVED in upstream-bound request (security boundary).
  - Upstream-down → 502 to client + record-with-Status=0 (operator sees what hit the proxy even when upstream fails); proxy.failures counter increments.
  - Hop-by-hop headers stripped from log (Connection dropped, X-Custom preserved).
  - LogWriter queue-full drop counter: 100 enqueues into queue-size-2 → written + dropped sums to 100, both nonzero.
  - Body truncation: MaxBodyLen=8 + 26-char body → captured body ends with "<truncated>" suffix.
  - LogWriter.Close idempotent (second call no-ops, doesn't deadlock); Enqueue-after-Close returns false.
  - Append-mode: two open-write-close cycles → 2 entries in file (not 1, not 0 — proves O_APPEND).
  - Proxy stats counter: 5 requests → proxy.Requests=5.
  - 1MB response body streamed (not buffered — would OOM if buffered).
  - singleJoin, stripHopHeaders, WriterStats.String roundtrip.

## Phase 5.J242 — Phase 6.3 nightly contract-suite CI workflow — 2026-05-26

Fourth Phase 6 prep slice. Workflow YAML only — no Go code change. Per PHASE_6_SCOPE.md § 6.3:

> The existing contract harness (`test/contract/replayer`) already self-skips when `-contract.base` is unset. Phase 6 turns this on in nightly CI: run the contract suite against a freshly-built Go binary at staging URL; run the same suite against the C# binary (also nightly-built); surface drift the moment any byte-equal endpoint regresses. This is purely CI plumbing — no Go code change needed beyond a workflow file.

J242 ships exactly that. The PR-triggered `contract-replay` job in `build_go.yml` covers same-PR drift; the nightly workflow covers external drift (upstream Sonarr commits between PR runs, dependency updates, environmental drift in long-running staging deploys).

Architecture (`.github/workflows/nightly-contract.yml`, 4 jobs):

  1. **preflight** — gates on `CONTRACT_STAGING_BASE_GO` + `CONTRACT_STAGING_BASE_CSHARP` repo secrets via `outputs.run_go` / `outputs.run_csharp`. When unset (the typical fork case) the gated jobs no-op cleanly via `if: needs.preflight.outputs.run_go == 'true'`. Workflow no-ops on forks rather than failing — that's the right default for "deploy infra you don't have."

  2. **go-staging** — verifies the staging deploy reachable via `curl -fsS .../ping` (fails fast on staging outage). Replays the contract corpus via `go test ./test/contract/replayer/... -contract.base=$BASE -contract.api-key=$KEY -contract.golden=... -contract.corpus=... -run TestReplay -v | tee /tmp/replay-go.out`. Counts "contract drift" lines via `grep -c "contract drift" /tmp/replay-go.out`. Gates against `CONTRACT_DRIFT_BASELINE=9` (matching the existing build_go.yml baseline established at J217). On drift > baseline → `::error::` + job fail; on drift < baseline → `::warning::` suggesting the operator lower the baseline to keep the guard tight. Step-summary contributes a "Go staging replay" section with drift + baseline. Replay log uploaded as artifact (14-day retention).

  3. **csharp-staging** — does the same replay against `CONTRACT_STAGING_BASE_CSHARP`. Does NOT gate against the drift baseline because C# IS the canonical reference — any drift here means the golden corpus is stale relative to live C# rather than a port gap. Step-summary frames the drift count as "corpus health check" — a signal to re-record against the latest upstream SHA. Artifact uploaded same as Go side.

  4. **diff-summary** — runs `if: always() && needs.go-staging.result == 'success' && needs.csharp-staging.result == 'success'` so it gathers both backend results when both succeed. Computes `DELTA = GO_DRIFT - CSHARP_DRIFT` and emits a cross-backend table. `DELTA <= 0` → "Go-port is at or ahead of the C# canonical." `DELTA > 0` → "Go-port has N more drifting endpoints than C#. Each is a Go-side wire-shape gap." This is the headline number an operator reads from the daily summary.

Triggers:

  - `schedule: cron: "0 3 * * *"` — 03:00 UTC daily. Quiet hour for upstream Sonarr work and most fork CI windows.
  - `workflow_dispatch` — manual debug invocation. Includes an `override_baseline` input so the operator can probe with a different baseline value without editing the file.

Concurrency: `group: nightly-contract`, `cancel-in-progress: false`. Prevents nightly overlap if a prior run is still draining — finish what you started before launching the next nightly tick.

Reuses the established drift-count extraction pattern from `build_go.yml`'s `contract-replay` job:

```
go test ... -run TestReplay -v 2>&1 | tee /tmp/replay.out || true
DRIFT=$(grep -c "contract drift" /tmp/replay.out || true)
```

The `|| true` after the `go test` pipeline is intentional — `TestReplaySkipsWhenUnconfigured` is the only test name and it FAILS by design when `-contract.base` is set (the test's contract is "skip when unset; assert that we did skip" — when configured the assertion fails). The workflow extracts drift count from stdout via grep rather than from the test exit code. Known-working hack since J217-era contract harness. Same pattern in the new workflow.

Hard gates: YAML syntax parses (`python3 -c "import yaml; yaml.safe_load(...)"` clean); job structure inspected (4 jobs, 2 triggers). No `actionlint` available locally to run a deeper static check — the workflow will get its first deep validation when GitHub Actions ingests it on next push.

Net diff: ~145 lines of YAML (single new file); PROGRESS.md update; STATUS.md slice note.

Safe to merge today even before staging URLs exist:

  - `CONTRACT_STAGING_BASE_GO` unset → go-staging job skipped via `if: needs.preflight.outputs.run_go == 'true'`.
  - `CONTRACT_STAGING_BASE_CSHARP` unset → csharp-staging job skipped.
  - Both skipped → diff-summary won't run because of the `needs:` chain.
  - Workflow exit: clean preflight job only. No errors, no warnings.

When the team provisions staging URLs, set the two secrets + the API key, the nightly fires automatically next 03:00 UTC.

## Phase 5.J243 — Shared `cmd/internal/shadowtraffic/httputil` package (dedup singleJoin + isHopHeader)

Three Phase 6.1 binaries (`cmd/shadow-traffic-diff` / `cmd/shadow-traffic-replay` / `cmd/shadow-traffic-record`) each kept byte-identical copies of two helpers:

```go
func singleJoin(base, req string) string { ... }
func isHopHeader(h string) bool { ... }
```

The replay binary's copy even carried the comment "matches the helper in cmd/shadow-traffic-diff/proxy.go" and the record binary's copy noted "keeping each cmd self-contained matters more than DRY here." Three implementations is the threshold at which the "keep self-contained" argument loses weight — any future hop-by-hop header list change has to land in three files, and the C# upstream's `WebSocketHandler` precedent (RFC 9110 §7.6.1 added `Proxy-Connection` to some lists) suggests this list isn't static.

J243 consolidates.

### Package location: `cmd/internal/shadowtraffic/httputil/`

The autonomous-loop prompt's slice-(A) suggested `cmd/shadowtraffic/internal/httputil/`. That path is structurally broken: Go's `internal/` rule scopes imports to the parent of `internal/`, which would be `cmd/shadowtraffic/`. The three consumers live at `cmd/shadow-traffic-diff/`, `cmd/shadow-traffic-replay/`, `cmd/shadow-traffic-record/` — siblings, not children of `cmd/shadowtraffic/`. Per Go's spec, a `cmd/shadowtraffic/internal/httputil` import from `cmd/shadow-traffic-diff` would error with `use of internal package not allowed`.

The fix is to scope `internal/` to a common ancestor: `cmd/internal/shadowtraffic/httputil/`. Anything under `cmd/*` (including all three binaries) can import; nothing else can. Same encapsulation guarantee, working import path.

### Package contents (`httputil.go` ~45 LOC + `httputil_test.go` ~60 LOC)

```go
// Package httputil holds tiny HTTP helpers shared across the
// cmd/shadow-traffic-{diff,replay,record} binaries.
package httputil

func SingleJoin(base, req string) string {
    if base == "" || base == "/" { return req }
    if base[len(base)-1] == '/' && len(req) > 0 && req[0] == '/' {
        return base + req[1:]
    }
    return base + req
}

func IsHopHeader(h string) bool {
    switch http.CanonicalHeaderKey(h) {
    case "Connection", "Keep-Alive", "Proxy-Authenticate", "Proxy-Authorization",
         "Te", "Trailers", "Transfer-Encoding", "Upgrade":
        return true
    }
    return false
}
```

Behaviour identical to the prior local copies. Both functions exported (capitalised) since they cross a package boundary now.

### Test coverage (broader than prior local tests)

The prior `TestSingleJoin` blocks tested 4-5 cases. The consolidated test covers 8 cases adding 3 edge cases the locals missed:

- `SingleJoin("/prefix", "")` → `"/prefix"` (empty req)
- `SingleJoin("", "")` → `""` (both empty)
- `SingleJoin("/", "")` → `""` (slash base with empty req — exercises the `base == "/"` short-circuit with falsy req)

`TestIsHopHeader` is brand new (no binary had one) and covers:

- 10 hop-positive cases: each canonical name + 3 case-variants on `Connection` (lowercase, uppercase, canonical) to pin `CanonicalHeaderKey` behaviour.
- 8 hop-negative cases including the substring-trap `X-Connection-Hint` (the name contains "Connection" but is not the literal "Connection" header — must not match) + empty string + `Host` + `Content-Length` (intentionally NOT in the hop list — both proxies strip it via a separate explicit check).

### Per-binary call-site rewires

`cmd/shadow-traffic-diff/proxy.go`:
- Added `"sonarr.tv/sonarr/cmd/internal/shadowtraffic/httputil"` import.
- 3 call sites: `isHopHeader(k)` → `httputil.IsHopHeader(k)` (twice for request + response header filtering) and `singleJoin(target.Path, src.URL.Path)` → `httputil.SingleJoin(...)`.
- 17 lines of local `singleJoin` + `isHopHeader` definitions removed.

`cmd/shadow-traffic-diff/proxy_test.go`:
- 14-line local `TestSingleJoin` removed (covered by shared package now).

`cmd/shadow-traffic-record/proxy.go`:
- Same import added.
- 3 call sites updated (request `isHopHeader` filter + response `isHopHeader || Content-Length` filter + `singleJoin(p.Upstream.Path, r.URL.Path)`).
- 22-line local helper block + comment removed.

`cmd/shadow-traffic-record/writer.go`:
- Same import added.
- 1 call site in `stripHopHeaders` body updated (it iterates the captured header map and skips hop-by-hops before writing to the JSONL log).
- `stripHopHeaders` itself stays local — it's a record-specific helper that also applies the `-drop-api-keys` security policy + the "single representative value per key" projection. Not a general HTTP utility.

`cmd/shadow-traffic-record/proxy_test.go`:
- 13-line local `TestSingleJoin` removed.
- `TestStripHopHeaders` retained (it tests the record-specific stripHopHeaders, which still lives in writer.go).

`cmd/shadow-traffic-replay/replay.go`:
- Same import added.
- 3 call sites: 2 `singleJoin` calls in URL composition (one for path-only, one for path-stripped-of-query) + 1 `isHopHeader || Host || Content-Length` filter in the replay-request header copier.
- 18-line local helper block + comment removed.

`cmd/shadow-traffic-replay/replay_test.go`:
- No `TestSingleJoin` to delete — replay never had one (was tested implicitly through the end-to-end replay-against-target tests).

### Why `stripHopHeaders` stays local to record

The shared package could expose `StripHopHeaders(headers, dropAPIKeys) map[string]string` as a third helper. Decision: NO — it mixes 3 concerns (hop filtering + API-key dropping + "single representative value per key" map projection) and only the record binary uses all three. The diff and replay binaries DO filter hop-by-hops but they preserve multi-value headers and don't apply the API-key drop. Generalising `stripHopHeaders` into a shared helper would either parameterise it heavily (4+ flags) or split it into a chain — both worse than the current scoped helper. The smaller `IsHopHeader` primitive is the right shared seam; the record-binary keeps its sanitization layer on top.

```

Roughly +105 LOC (shared package, mostly tests) − ~85 LOC (3 binaries' duplicates + 2 dropped tests) = ~+20 LOC net for a more thoroughly tested + structurally consolidated shared seam.

## Phase 5.J244 — gzip request body decompression on shadow-traffic-record

### Why

The Phase 6.1 recorder (J241) tees client requests into a JSONL log file for later replay or operator inspection. When the client (e.g. a curl script gzipping its payload to save bandwidth) sends `Content-Encoding: gzip`, the captured `Body` field in the log was the raw gzipped bytes. Replay round-trips this fine — it sends those same bytes back upstream with the same `Content-Encoding: gzip` header. But the operator opening the log file saw gzip garbage and couldn't tell what was actually posted. For a port-validation toolkit (which is what 6.1 is) this matters — the whole point is for a human to inspect captured production traffic and confirm the Go-port behaves the same as C#.

Sonarr's stock UI doesn't gzip request bodies, but operators-in-the-wild scripts sometimes do (the manualimport/customformat-bulk endpoints take large JSON bodies that compress 5-10x), and the recorder is also used in capture-from-anywhere scenarios where the upstream client is not under the team's control.

### Design

The minimum-invasive change:

1. Decompress gzipped request bodies into `RecordedEntry.Body` BEFORE writing to JSONL.
2. Strip `Content-Encoding` from the captured `Headers` map (otherwise the header would lie about the now-plain body bytes — replay would try to gunzip plain JSON and fail).
3. Crucially: do NOT alter the upstream-bound bytes. The proxy must remain semantically transparent — upstream receives the byte-identical original payload, the same `Content-Encoding` header, and behaves exactly as if the recorder weren't in the path.
4. Malformed gzip degrades cleanly: body stays in the log verbatim, `Content-Encoding` header retained (because the body IS still gzip-tagged garbage — the header is truthful).
5. Decompression-bomb guard: a 1KB gzip can expand to gigabytes. Cap the decompressed output and fall back to verbatim logging if exceeded.

### Code

`writer.go` gains the helper `maybeDecompressForLog(body, contentEncoding, limit)` (~35 LOC). Only gzip is decoded (case-insensitive); `deflate` and `br` aren't on the table because Sonarr's API doesn't emit either in practice. Empty body with gzip encoding degrades to (empty, false) — no point trying to read a gzip stream from zero bytes. The `limit+1` then `>` check is the standard idiom for "did the input exceed the cap" — `io.LimitReader` returns up to limit+1 bytes; if we got exactly limit+1, the source had more. `gzip.NewReader` validates the header — non-gzip bytes return `gzip.ErrHeader` immediately; no panic risk.

`stripHopHeaders` extended with a third parameter `dropContentEncoding bool`. The recorder sets it when decompression actually succeeded; the captured header would otherwise lie about the now-plain body bytes.

`proxy.go` `record()` calls `maybeDecompressForLog` against `r.Header.Get("Content-Encoding")` with the writer's `maxBodyLen` (or 8 MiB default) as the decompression cap, propagates the success flag to `stripHopHeaders`, and emits a warn-log on decompression skip when the header actually said gzip + body was non-empty (the "something went wrong" case worth noticing; empty body or non-gzip encoding are quiet skips). A small `decompressLimitFor(w *LogWriter) int64` ladder picks the writer's `maxBodyLen` if set (keeping the decompression cap aligned with the existing body-truncation threshold) otherwise the 8 MiB default — sufficient for any realistic Sonarr POST body (the largest stock UI submissions are manualimport JSON at <500 KiB).

### Upstream is NOT touched (the critical invariant)

The existing dispatch path uses the ORIGINAL buffered `body []byte` — the same gzipped bytes the client sent. The decompression in `record()` only affects what gets written to the JSONL log; the variable `body` itself is never mutated. Upstream sees `Content-Encoding: gzip` + the original gzipped payload. The recorder is semantically transparent.

The end-to-end test `TestRecordingProxy_GzipRequestBody_DecompressedInLog_VerbatimToUpstream` pins this invariant via two assertions: upstream-side, the test handler reads the request body and atomically flags whether it byte-equals the original gzipped bytes the client sent; log-side, the JSONL Body must equal the plain JSON. If either fails, the slice has regressed.

### Tests

10 net test additions (6 brand new + 4 updates to existing TestStripHopHeaders to cover Content-Encoding scenarios):

- `TestMaybeDecompressForLog_Gzip` — happy-path round-trip on a hand-built gzip stream containing a small JSON object.
- `TestMaybeDecompressForLog_GzipCaseInsensitive` — `gzip` / `GZIP` / `Gzip` all match (RFC 9110 makes the header value case-insensitive).
- `TestMaybeDecompressForLog_NoGzip` — empty encoding and `Content-Encoding: identity` both return (original, false) without mutating the body.
- `TestMaybeDecompressForLog_MalformedGzip` — bytes that don't form a valid gzip stream return (original, false) rather than panicking. Tested with arbitrary text AND with nil body — both degrade cleanly.
- `TestMaybeDecompressForLog_BombGuard` — gzip that decompresses to 2 KiB, tested with limit=1024 (over-limit → falls back to verbatim) and limit=4096 (under-limit → decompresses cleanly). Both cases exercised.
- `TestRecordingProxy_GzipRequestBody_DecompressedInLog_VerbatimToUpstream` — end-to-end through the proxy: client POSTs gzipped JSON; verifies (a) upstream received original gzipped bytes via atomic.Bool flag in the test handler, (b) JSONL log entry has decompressed JSON in `Body`, (c) `Content-Encoding` absent from log's `Headers` map.
- `TestRecordingProxy_PlainRequestBody_RecordedVerbatim_NoEncodingHeader` — sanity check: a non-gzip POST is still recorded verbatim with original `Content-Type` (no regression in the no-encoding path).
- `TestRecordingProxy_GzipMalformedBody_LoggedVerbatim_HeaderRetained` — adversarial: `Content-Encoding: gzip` but the body isn't valid gzip. Verifies (a) no panic, (b) log body has original bytes verbatim, (c) `Content-Encoding` STAYS in the log headers (still truthful — the body IS gzip-tagged garbage), (d) upstream received original bytes.
- `TestStripHopHeaders` updated — input map gained a `Content-Encoding: gzip` row; new assertions test both directions of the `dropContentEncoding` flag.

Subtle test-infrastructure gotcha worth recording: my first draft of the malformed-gzip end-to-end test used the gzip magic prefix bytes followed by ASCII garbage as the payload, figuring it would be a realistic "looks like gzip but isn't" probe. But the second magic byte (0x8b) is an invalid UTF-8 continuation byte without a start byte, and the JSONL log uses `json.Marshal` which silently replaces invalid UTF-8 with the Unicode replacement character U+FFFD. The round-trip through JSON mangled the bytes, and the assertion `entries[0].Body != string(garbage)` triggered a false-positive failure. Switched the garbage payload to pure ASCII ("not actually gzipped data") and the test passes. Lesson noted inline: log bodies are JSON-encoded, so binary payloads need UTF-8-safe test fixtures unless you explicitly want to test the lossy round-trip.

### Hard gates

```
$ go build ./...
(clean)

$ go vet ./...
(clean)

$ go test -race -count=1 ./cmd/shadow-traffic-record/...
ok  sonarr.tv/sonarr/cmd/shadow-traffic-record  1.496s
```

All tests pass under -race (test count grew by 6 new + 4 reinforcements via the TestStripHopHeaders expansion).

- (D) Shadow-traffic toolkit FORMAT.md (`go/cmd/shadow-traffic-record/FORMAT.md` documenting the JSONL log schema). Pure docs work.

## Phase 5.J245 — Shadow-traffic JSONL FORMAT.md

### Why

Phase 6.1's three binaries (J239 diff / J240 replay / J241 record) communicate via a one-line-per-entry JSONL file. Field shapes are documented in code (the `LogEntry` / `RecordedEntry` struct doc-comments at `cmd/shadow-traffic-replay/log.go:21-45` and `cmd/shadow-traffic-record/writer.go:34-41`) but only mentioned in narrative form across the J239/J240/J241/J244 STATUS slices. Operators editing logs by hand — the realistic Phase 6 workflow when scripting probes or pruning a recorded session — need a single-source reference rather than having to grep four commits' worth of free-form prose.

J245 lands that reference: `cmd/shadow-traffic-record/FORMAT.md` is the authoritative per-field schema. The doc is co-located with the recorder (the binary that writes the format) and explicitly labels itself secondary to the code — if it disagrees with `writer.go` or `replay.go`, the code wins and the doc is the bug.

### What's in it

Sections:

1. **File shape** — JSONL conventions: one JSON object per non-blank, non-comment line, no surrounding brackets, append-only, 4 MiB max-line cap.
2. **Per-entry schema** — six-row table covering `ts` / `method` / `path` / `headers` / `body` / `status` with JSON type, tag (including the subtle `ts` tag difference between recorder's `json:"ts"` and replay's `json:"ts,omitzero"`), required-or-optional, and operational meaning.
3. **Minimal entries** — the smallest legal entry (just `method` + `path`).
4. **Body encoding** — UTF-8 caveat (json.Marshal mangles non-UTF-8 bytes; cited as the lesson from the J244 test gotcha) + gzip in-place decompression contract (per J244: decompressed body + stripped Content-Encoding on success; verbatim body + retained Content-Encoding on malformed gzip).
5. **Headers map** — single-value-per-key map shape; what's stripped on capture (hop-by-hop per RFC 7230; API keys when `-drop-api-keys=true` default; Content-Encoding only when decompression succeeded); upstream still sees original headers verbatim (proxy transparency).
6. **Status=0 sentinel** — upstream-failure encoding via omitempty-elided field; `-status 0` filter targets only failures.
7. **Truncation marker** — literal `...<truncated>` ASCII sentinel; replay-incompatible (deliberate trade — truncation is an inspection knob, set `-max-body-len=0` for byte-perfect replay).
8. **Comments and blank lines** — reader-side conventions for hand-edited logs (lines starting with `#` skipped; whitespace-only lines skipped). Writer never emits them — they're for humans.
9. **Examples** — 7 worked entries: plain GET, POST with JSON body, originally-gzipped POST (showing Content-Encoding stripped), API-key-stripped POST, Status=0 upstream-unreachable, truncated body, hand-edited probe with no timestamp.
10. **Inter-tool contract** — 3-row matrix showing which binary reads/writes the format; clarifies that diff doesn't touch the format directly (it's a live reverse-proxy) but chains via `replay -target=<diff-listen-addr>` for log-driven diffing.
11. **Stability** — schema-evolution rules: additive `omitempty` fields are backward-compatible; mandatory-field additions break captures and would need a schema-version tag (none today — the format is small enough that operator inspection catches drift).

### Co-location vs central docs

The file goes at `cmd/shadow-traffic-record/FORMAT.md` rather than `go/docs/SHADOW_TRAFFIC_FORMAT.md` or similar central location. Reasoning: the record binary owns the on-disk format (it's the writer); the replay binary just consumes what the recorder produces. Anyone editing a JSONL log by hand has the record binary's source on screen at some point — the doc is two paths away (`-record/FORMAT.md`). The other two binaries cross-reference it via comment in their doc-comments (replay's `LogEntry` and diff's reverse-proxy code).

The alternative — putting it in `go/cmd/shadowtraffic/FORMAT.md` next to the J243 shared httputil package — was considered. Rejected: J243's shared package is a 45-LOC HTTP utility, not a tool-suite root. There's no `cmd/shadowtraffic/` directory housing the three binaries; they're siblings at `cmd/shadow-traffic-{record,replay,diff}/`. Co-location with the writer is the natural anchor.

### What this doc does NOT cover

- **CLI flags for the three binaries** — those are documented via `go run ./cmd/shadow-traffic-record -h` (and likewise for replay + diff). FORMAT.md only covers the on-disk format; not how operators invoke each tool.
- **Replay pacing semantics** — `-speed` multiplier, `-concurrency` worker pool, `-timeout` per-request — those are operational tuning knobs, not file-format concerns. They're covered in J240's STATUS slice.
- **Diff redaction rules** — `RedactConfig` JSON shape, default redact paths — those are diff-binary-specific and covered in J239's STATUS slice.
- **CI integration** — the Phase 6.3 nightly-contract workflow doesn't read or write this format directly; it shells out to the existing `test/contract/replayer` (a different binary with its own corpus format).

Boundary chosen deliberately: FORMAT.md is the file-format reference; per-tool operational behaviour stays in each tool's `-h` output + the J239/J240/J241/J244 STATUS slices.

### Code change

None. Pure markdown addition (~210 lines).

$ go build ./...
(clean)

$ go vet ./cmd/shadow-traffic-record/...
(clean)
```

No tests to run (no code change). The doc itself is self-validating in a small way: every example JSONL entry has been hand-checked against the live `RecordedEntry`/`LogEntry` schemas, including the subtle `ts` tag difference and the `status,omitempty` ≡ `status:0` equivalence.

## Phase 5.J246 — Phase 6.2 operator smoke runbook

### Why

The Phase 6 strategic plan ("Pre-cutover gate" in `~/.claude/plans/curried-discovering-meadow.md`) names three layers of pre-cutover validation:

| Layer  | Mechanism                          | Lands at  |
| ------ | ---------------------------------- | --------- |
| 6.1    | Shadow-traffic harness             | J239-J241 |
| 6.2    | Manual smoke checklist             | **J246**  |
| 6.3    | Nightly contract-suite CI          | J242      |

6.1 and 6.3 are automated; 6.2 is operator-driven. The strategic plan's exact phrasing — "Add a series, run a search, grab a release, import a file, send notifications, take a backup, restore the backup — end-to-end on both binaries with identical results" — is a seven-scenario checklist that needs to live somewhere committed so the operator running smoke isn't reinventing the steps each time.

### What J246 lands

`go/PHASE_6_SMOKE.md` — operator-facing runbook (~210 lines markdown). Co-located with `PHASE_6_SCOPE.md` so the doc tree under `go/` carries the full Phase 6 operational reference together. (Alternative locations considered: `docs/PHASE_6_SMOKE.md` rejected because `go/` doesn't have a `docs/` tree today; `cmd/sonarr/SMOKE.md` rejected because smoke is about the whole tree, not a single binary.)

Sections:

1. **Scope** — Seven scenarios in scope. Out-of-scope explicitly: performance benchmarking, live DB migration, UI pixel diff (separate runbooks). The boundary matters — without it, smoke-runbook scope-creep makes the gate unable to ever pass.
2. **Setup** — Two side-by-side binaries (C# at `:8989`, Go at `:8990`), fresh DBs on each. Two browser windows. Standardised result-recording fields (C# result, Go-port result, verdict).
3. **Verdict rubric** — PASS (user-visible behaviour equivalent), DIVERGE-LOW (cosmetic — timing, log wording), DIVERGE-HIGH (functional — different status code, missing field, persistence mismatch). DIVERGE-LOW doesn't block 6.4; DIVERGE-HIGH does.
4. **Seven scenarios** — Each gets: UI steps (clickable affordances), expected wire (specific API endpoints + status codes), expected UI behaviour, observable assertions, cross-binary verdict criteria.
5. **Reporting** — Operator writes `phase6-smoke-YYYY-MM-DD.md` in local notes (NOT committed — operator workspace). Tally per scenario. Smoke gate passes when `K=0 DIVERGE-HIGH AND M≤2 DIVERGE-LOW`.
6. **Layer-coverage table** — Explicitly contrasts what 6.1 + 6.3 + 6.2 each catch and miss. Headline insight: 6.1 + 6.3 see each individual API call in isolation; 6.2 catches multi-call workflow ordering bugs that the body diff can't see.
7. **Re-running cadence** — Before each 6.4 cutover attempt; after touching the listed internal/* packages; monthly during the shadow-traffic monitoring period.
8. **Open questions** — Backup format compatibility (cross-binary restore), notification provider account prereq, drop folder permissions.

### Port-history landmines surfaced as scenario-specific assertions

The runbook calls out specific scenarios where prior port slices fixed regressions the operator MUST verify on a real run:

- **Scenario 3 (Grab a release)**: Verifies the POST /api/v3/release path returns 200 (not 404). J237 introduced the in-memory release cache that fixed the "couldn't find requested release in cache, try searching again" 404 when the cache TTL ran out under bulk-grab flows. The contract harness wouldn't catch a cache-TTL regression — it only sees individual endpoint calls.
- **Scenario 4 (Import a file)**: Verifies POST /api/v3/manualimport returns 200 with non-empty `series` field. J238 wired the manualimport REPROCESS endpoint port; the runbook is the integration check that the wire-shape decisions made in J238 (CamelCaseEnumName + null-as-empty CustomFormats + folder-based series lookup) work end-to-end through the UI.
- **Scenario 5 (Test notifications, Pushover-specific)**: Verifies E2E encryption when `encryptionKey` is set. J219 wired the Pushover AES-256-CBC + HMAC-SHA256 + gzip envelope; the runbook is the integration check that the operator can configure a key in settings → click "Test" → receive an encrypted notification at the Pushover client.

These callouts make the runbook MORE than a generic functional check — it's a regression-verification gate specifically for the multi-call paths the contract harness can't reach.

### Why manual

The runbook is explicitly NOT automated. Reasoning:

- Automating the seven scenarios would re-implement the React UI in headless form (Playwright / Cypress / Selenium). That's a Phase 6.5 effort, not a Phase 6.2 effort.
- The signal-to-noise ratio of UI automation is poor for smoke testing — flakiness from CSS animations, timing, server start ordering. An hour of operator clicking is more reliable than 4 hours of CI debugging.
- The runbook is intentionally re-runnable monthly during the shadow-traffic monitoring period. A monthly cadence makes the manual cost acceptable; a per-commit cadence would not.
- Selenium-style automation also can't observe SignalR fan-out reliably without a custom WebSocket client — the simpler "operator watches the live UI update" check is more direct.

None. Pure markdown addition.

No tests to run (no code change). The runbook itself is self-validating: every wire-shape assertion in the seven scenarios maps to a specific port slice in `STATUS.md` (J39 for searches, J216 for SeriesAddCompletedEvent fan-out, J219 for Pushover, J237 for release cache, J238 for manualimport, etc.).

## Phase 5.J247 — Cross-tool integration smoke test for the shadow-traffic triad

### Why

The Phase 6.1 toolkit (J239 diff + J240 replay + J241 record) was built in three slices. Each had its own unit tests (HTTP-level tests within the binary's package). What was missing: a single test that proves the THREE binaries actually compose. Specifically:

- That `record`'s JSONL output is byte-shape-compatible with `replay`'s JSONL input (the schema documented in J245 FORMAT.md).
- That `replay` can drive `diff`'s listen addr without protocol mismatch.
- That `diff`'s downstream dispatch to two backends produces the diff-report shape the report.go writes (and that the operator would actually open).
- That the SIGTERM-flush invariants on `record` + `diff` actually work when invoked from a subprocess parent.

Each binary's unit tests assume an in-process composition. The real Phase 6.1 deployment is three separate processes communicating via file + HTTP. The integration test pins that mode.

### Test shape

`cmd/shadowtraffic-e2e/e2e_test.go`. Package `shadowtraffic_e2e` (test-only — `doc.go` carries the package declaration for `go build ./...` cleanliness). Run via `go test ./cmd/shadowtraffic-e2e/...`.

Two tests:

**TestTriadComposesEndToEnd** — the full end-to-end:

1. Two `httptest.NewServer` fakes: fake C# returns `{"server":"csharp","id":1}`; fake Go returns `{"server":"go","id":1}` — value-only diff to exercise the LOW-severity classification path (the J239 differ classifies field-presence/type mismatches as HIGH and value-only mismatches as LOW).
2. Start `shadow-traffic-record` fronting fake C#; `-flush-interval 50ms`, `-sync-on-close true`, `-stats-interval 1h` (the last to suppress periodic stats noise that would otherwise litter test stderr).
3. Drive 3 GET requests at the record's front. Each request asserts the client sees the C# response body (proving record's reverse-proxy forwarding works under subprocess spawn).
4. SIGTERM record. The graceful-shutdown path flushes the JSONL log to disk + closes cleanly.
5. Read the JSONL log via the test's `readJSONL` helper (which respects FORMAT.md's blank+comment-line conventions). Assert 3 entries with `method=GET` + `path=/api/v3/series`.
6. Start `shadow-traffic-diff` with both fakes wired as `-primary-url` (C#) + `-secondary-url` (Go); `-flush-interval 200ms` keeps the report-flush cadence test-friendly.
7. Reset the fake-backend hit counters.
8. Run `shadow-traffic-replay` with `-log` pointing at record's output + `-target` pointing at diff's listen addr + `-speed 0` (no throttling). Replay's `main.go` exits on log EOF, so the parent test just `Wait()`s.
9. Assert both fakes saw 3 hits each. This proves diff's dual-dispatch fan-out works (each inbound request → both backends in parallel).
10. Sleep 600ms (one flush-interval + safety margin) so the diff's async report-writer drains.
11. SIGTERM diff. Final flush on shutdown.
12. Glob `*.diffs.jsonl` files in the report-dir; expect at least one. Decode each row to a map; expect at least one row whose JSON contains both "server" and either "csharp" or "go" (the value diff).

**TestRecordReplayRoundTripsCleanly** — the narrower companion. Isolates the record↔replay format contract from the diff binary so a failure points at one half vs the other:

1. One backend instead of two; it appends every received request shape to a slice (Method + Path + Body) protected by a channel-based mutex.
2. Run record → drive 3 probes (GET / POST with body / DELETE).
3. SIGTERM record. Snapshot the backend's recording-phase capture.
4. Run replay against the SAME backend (`-target=backend.URL`).
5. Backend's replay-phase capture must byte-equal the recording-phase capture probe-by-probe.

Why two tests: when (TestTriadComposesEndToEnd) fails, it could be any of three binaries; when (TestRecordReplayRoundTripsCleanly) ALSO fails, the bug is in record or replay; when only the e2e test fails, the bug is in diff or in how diff consumes replay's output. Bisects the failure space.

### TestMain — build once, share across tests

```go
func TestMain(m *testing.M) {
    tmp, _ := os.MkdirTemp("", "shadowtraffic-e2e-bins-")
    for _, name := range []string{"shadow-traffic-diff", "shadow-traffic-replay", "shadow-traffic-record"} {
        out := filepath.Join(tmp, name)
        build := exec.Command("go", "build", "-o", out, "sonarr.tv/sonarr/cmd/"+name)
        // ... run build, populate binaries map
    }
    code := m.Run()
    _ = os.RemoveAll(tmp)
    os.Exit(code)
}
```

Three binaries built once per `go test` invocation; both tests share. Build failure aborts the whole test run with a clear stderr message. Tmpdir cleaned even when tests panic (defer-equivalent ordering: m.Run returns → cleanup → os.Exit).

### Helpers

- `pickPort(t)` — `net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0")`, capture port, immediately close. The kernel may reassign the port before the binary binds, but the race window is tiny and 2 ports per test run is well within tolerance. (Alternative: pass `-listen :0` to the binary and have it print the actual port — would require changes to all three binaries. Out of scope for a test scaffold.)
- `waitListening(t, addr, max)` — poll-connect with 20ms ticks until something accepts or deadline. Replaces the brittle "sleep 200ms after Start" pattern.
- `stopAndWait(t, cmd, name)` — SIGTERM + 5s grace + Kill fallback. Logs (doesn't fail) on non-clean exit because the binaries' SIGTERM handlers DO exit cleanly via the signal-handler block — but a Kill fallback ExitError still passes through `Wait()`, and that's fine; we assert on output not exit codes.
- `readJSONL(t, path)` — reads a JSONL file, skips blank + `#`-prefixed lines per FORMAT.md, decodes each remaining line to `map[string]any`. Test-side mirror of the recorder's writer + replayer's reader; if FORMAT.md is wrong, all three of (recorder writes / replayer reads / readJSONL parses) diverge and the test will catch it.

### Honours `-short`

Both tests start with `if testing.Short() { t.Skip(...) }`. The reasoning: the e2e tests spawn 3 subprocesses + 2 `httptest` servers and consume ~5 seconds of wallclock. The existing fast-unit-test sweep (`go test -short ./...`) shouldn't pay that cost on every CI run. The e2e tests run on `go test ./...` (the default), so any commit touching the three binaries triggers the integration check; `-short` is the escape hatch for developers iterating on unrelated packages.

### Why ~440 LOC instead of the prompt's "~150 LOC"

The prompt estimated ~150 LOC. Actual: ~440 LOC. The overage is in scaffolding, not assertions:

- TestMain + binaries map + helpers (~110 LOC) — could be skipped if all three binaries were in the same package, but they're three separate `main` packages requiring subprocess spawn.
- Per-test subprocess lifecycle (~40 LOC each across two tests = 80 LOC) — Start + waitListening + drive traffic + SIGTERM + cleanup deferred for failure path.
- Per-test response handling + flush-timing waits (~40 LOC each = 80 LOC).
- Two tests instead of one (~80 LOC for the second). Could have collapsed to one larger test but the bisect-the-failure-space argument carried the day.
- Assertions + comments inline with steps (~90 LOC).

The prompt's "~150 LOC" estimate assumed the tests would be one function with minimal scaffolding. The reality of multi-binary integration testing — port allocation, process lifecycle, output assertion across binaries that don't share types — needed more infrastructure.

### Subtle correctness notes

- **Diff binary returns the PRIMARY response to the caller.** During TestTriadComposesEndToEnd step 8 (replay drives diff), replay's HTTP requests get back the C# response body (because diff streams primary's response to the caller). The Go fake's response is only consumed by diff's background diff-goroutine. We assert on hit counts (both backends got 3 hits) rather than on response bodies because the response bodies are by-design "primary wins."
- **Diff's flush is async + interval-driven.** The `-flush-interval 200ms` flag drives when the in-memory report buffer is written to disk. Step 10 sleeps 600ms (3x the interval) before reading reports — defensive, accommodates scheduling jitter on busy test runners.
- **SIGTERM forces final flush.** Step 11 SIGTERMs diff before reading reports, even though step 10 already waited for the interval flush. The graceful-shutdown path is the safety net for "what if a report was generated in the last 200ms and the interval-flush missed it."
- **Mutex via channel-as-semaphore.** TestRecordReplayRoundTripsCleanly uses `var mu = make(chan struct{}, 1); mu <- struct{}{}` rather than `sync.Mutex`. Reason: the test reads + writes a slice from inside an HTTP handler goroutine while the main test goroutine reads the snapshot. Channel-mutex makes the synchronisation visible at the call sites (`<-mu` / `mu <- struct{}{}`) which is helpful for the integration-test reader who's already context-switching across three binaries' worth of code.

### Hard gates

```
$ go build ./...
(clean)

$ go vet ./...
(clean)

$ go test -race -count=1 -timeout 120s ./cmd/shadowtraffic-e2e/...
ok  sonarr.tv/sonarr/cmd/shadowtraffic-e2e  4.892s
```

Both tests pass under -race in under 5 seconds. The build-binaries-in-TestMain dominates the wallclock (3x `go build` calls); the actual subprocess orchestration is sub-second per test.

- (B) [CLOSED at J244] gzip body decompression on shadow-traffic-record.
- (C) [CLOSED at J246] Phase 6.2 smoke runbook scaffold.
- (D) [CLOSED at J245] Shadow-traffic JSONL FORMAT.md.

- **Phase 6.4 cutover commit** — gated on 14+ days of zero unexplained diff in the 6.1 shadow-traffic daily reports; needs staging URLs + the nightly contract gate (J242) actively gating real traffic.

## Phase 5.J248 — Windows getActualCasing impl (Wave 1 deferred sub-arc)

### Why

J208 closed the path-canonicalisation arc with `normalizePath(path) (string, error)` as the always-on first half of C# `RefreshSeriesService.cs:118` (`new DirectoryInfo(series.Path).FullName`), AND with `getActualCasing(path) string` as a no-op stub on all platforms — the second half. The C# extension at `PathExtensions.cs:213-236` is genuinely no-op on non-Windows (short-circuits via `if OsInfo.IsNotWindows`), so the J208 stub matched C# verbatim for the Linux containers Sonarr primarily runs on. Windows behaviour was deferred per the J208 doc-comment: "When that slice lands it can split this function into build-tagged files (`pathcasing_windows.go` + `pathcasing_other.go`) without changing the call site at RefreshSeriesInfo."

J248 lands that split. The user-visible payoff is small (a Sonarr install on Windows that has a series Path entered in non-canonical casing — e.g. `C:\\media\\BREAKING.BAD\\` vs the on-disk `C:\\Media\\Breaking.Bad\\` — will now have the persisted Path normalised to the on-disk form). But the slice mainly closes a captured-during-completion debt item — the kind of TODO that erodes confidence in the port if it lingers.

### Structure

Three files under `internal/refreshseries/`:

**`pathcasing.go`** (always-on) — keeps `normalizePath` from J208 verbatim, removes the `getActualCasing` stub, adds the new `caseFixWalker(path, readDir)` helper. Signature uses `io/fs.DirEntry` rather than `os.DirEntry` so the readDir callback is injectable (tests pass fakes; live callers pass `os.ReadDir` adapted via a one-line closure).

```go
func caseFixWalker(path string, readDir func(string) ([]fs.DirEntry, error)) string {
    parent := filepath.Dir(path)
    if parent == path {
        return strings.ToUpper(path)
    }
    name := filepath.Base(path)
    parentCased := caseFixWalker(parent, readDir)
    if entries, err := readDir(parentCased); err == nil {
        for _, e := range entries {
            if strings.EqualFold(e.Name(), name) {
                return filepath.Join(parentCased, e.Name())
            }
        }
    }
    return filepath.Join(parentCased, name)
}
```

Ports the C# `GetProperCapitalization` recursion at `:194-211`. Behaviour rules pinned verbatim from C#:

- Root segment (when `filepath.Dir(p) == p` — drive letter on Windows or `/` on POSIX) gets `strings.ToUpper` applied. Matches C# `:199 dirInfo.Name.ToUpper()`. On POSIX `strings.ToUpper("/") == "/"` so this is a no-op for the root step.
- Non-root segments: ReadDir the case-corrected parent, scan for case-insensitive name match, use on-disk casing if found.
- ReadDir failure (permission denied, parent missing) → preserve input casing for that segment + continue walking down with case-corrected ancestor prefix. Matches the absorb-and-keep-walking posture C# relies on (DirectoryInfo doesn't throw for missing parents).
- No case-insensitive match in readDir output → preserve input casing for that segment. Matches C# `:204-207` where `folderName` defaults to `dirInfo.Name`.

**`pathcasing_other.go`** (`//go:build !windows`) — three-line no-op `getActualCasing`. Mirrors C# `:215-218` (`if OsInfo.IsNotWindows`). POSIX filesystems are typically case-sensitive (ext4 / XFS / APFS-default) so on-disk casing IS the input casing; nothing to recover.

**`pathcasing_windows.go`** (`//go:build windows`) — real entry point:

```go
func getActualCasing(path string) string {
    if len(path) == 0 {
        return path
    }
    if path[0] == '\\' || path[0] == '/' {
        return path
    }
    return caseFixWalker(path, func(p string) ([]fs.DirEntry, error) {
        return os.ReadDir(p)
    })
}
```

The UNC + leading-slash bail matches C# `:215-218 path.StartsWith("\\")`. C# additionally bails on bare leading-backslash relative paths (`\foo`) — Go has the same guard. The extra `/` guard is defensive in case Go's path normalisation converted a separator inbound; doesn't change C# semantics on Windows where `\\` is the canonical form.

### Why the algorithm lives outside the build-tagged files

Two reasons:

1. **Cross-platform unit testability.** With `caseFixWalker` always-on, tests inject a fake `readDir` from a `map[parent][]name` fixture and exercise every behaviour rule (recovery, missing segment, no match, root uppercase, always-fail) on the dev's macOS box. Without this extraction the Windows-only code would be untestable until someone boots a Windows VM.
2. **Future-proofing.** If a similar parent-walk casing recovery becomes useful in a Linux context (e.g. case-insensitive filesystem mounts like exFAT or NTFS-over-CIFS), the algorithm is already isolated and can be wired without rewriting.

### Tests

**`pathcasing_test.go`** (cross-platform, 5 new tests via fake readDir):

- `TestCaseFixWalker_RecoversOnDiskCasing` — happy path: fixture has `/tmp/Refresh/Show`; input `/tmp/REFRESH/show` returns `/tmp/Refresh/Show`. Mirrors C# regression test at `PathExtensionFixture.cs:247-263`.
- `TestCaseFixWalker_PreservesInputOnMissingSegment` — fixture has `/tmp/Refresh` but no entries below; input `/tmp/REFRESH/show` returns `/tmp/Refresh/show` (parent recovered, tail preserved).
- `TestCaseFixWalker_PreservesInputOnNoMatch` — fixture has `/tmp/OtherDir` but no "Refresh" entry; input `/tmp/refresh` returns `/tmp/refresh` verbatim.
- `TestCaseFixWalker_UppercasesRoot` — exercises the `ToUpper(root)` rule via a path that recurses to "/". POSIX `ToUpper("/") == "/"` so this also serves as a no-regression guard on the root step.
- `TestCaseFixWalker_ReadDirAlwaysErrors` — every parent lookup returns `fs.ErrPermission`; every segment retains input casing.

The fake readDir builds `fs.DirEntry` instances via a small `fakeEntry` struct implementing the interface (Name + IsDir + Type + Info methods). Path keys in the fixture use `/` so the tests run identically on macOS and Linux without separator conditionals.

**`pathcasing_other_test.go`** (`//go:build !windows`, 1 test) — re-pins the no-op contract on POSIX builds. Without this the contract would be implicit ("trust the algorithm wasn't run"); with it the contract is explicit ("verified the function returns input verbatim for these inputs").

**`pathcasing_windows_test.go`** (`//go:build windows`, 5 tests, real filesystem) — integration tests that only run on Windows hosts:

- `TestGetActualCasing_WalksParents` — creates `<tmp>/MixedCase/SubDir/Leaf.txt`; asserts `getActualCasing("<tmp>/MIXEDCASE/subdir/LEAF.txt")` returns the canonical form.
- `TestGetActualCasing_PreservesNonExistentTail` — creates `<tmp>/RealParent`; asserts `getActualCasing("<tmp>/realparent/doesNotExist.txt")` recovers the parent casing but preserves the non-existent tail.
- `TestGetActualCasing_UNCReturnsUnchanged` — pins the `\\\\server\\share\\...` + `\\foo\\bar` bail.
- `TestGetActualCasing_Empty` — empty string returns empty string (avoids crash inside `filepath.Dir` recursion).
- `TestGetActualCasing_UppercaseDriveLetter` — mangle the temp dir drive letter to lowercase, walk back, assert the result starts with the upper-cased letter + colon. Skips if the temp dir isn't on a drive letter (CI runners on Linux that somehow ran the Windows test would skip cleanly).

The Windows tests use `t.TempDir()` which on Windows lives on the drive the OS configured. No cleanup needed — `t.TempDir` handles removal.

### Hard gates

Native (host macOS):

```
$ go build ./...
(clean)

$ go vet ./internal/refreshseries/...
(clean)

$ go test -race -count=1 ./internal/refreshseries/...
ok  sonarr.tv/sonarr/internal/refreshseries  1.662s
```
